text.p: NTT, the $160 billion Japanese telecoms titan, said on Monday it was focusing European investment plans on second carriers in the key markets of France and Germany.

Shuji Tomita, the managing director of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp's European operations, told Reuters that the company might invest in a company like France's Cegetel -- which has ambitions to establish a pan-European network -- or in telephone operators on a country-by-country basis.
"We're studying local investments in France and Germany," Tomita said. "(But) it's a large investment. It's a difficult decision."

Talks between NTT and Cegetel, which hopes to launch an attack on France Telecom's market share when the market is opened up to competition next year, have centred on NTT taking a stake of up to 9.9 percent in Cegetel's French railway venture, Telecom Developpement.

British Telecommunications Plc, which has been wooing NTT for years, has a 26 percent stake in Cegetel. It shares ownership with France's utility Cie Gnrale des Eaux, Germany's Mannesmann AG and America's SBC Communications Inc.

Beyond noting that negotiations were always "tough and difficult", Tomita said he knew no details about talks. He also declined to divulge who NTT was negotiating with in Germany or how large an investment NTT was considering.
"Certainly there is money in the pocket -- but that is not revealed," he said.
After 14 years of wrangling with the Japanese government, NTT was freed in January to pursue international business in return for an agreement to split itself into four units under a holding company.
NTT, which has set aside 100 billion yen for overseas projects in 1997/98, plans to start international services on September 1 and has set up a new division to spearhead its overseas strategy.

The group plans to provide Japanese corporate customers as well as European-based multinationals looking to expand into Asia with information and systems integration services by leasing lines from other operators.
NTT, the world's biggest telecoms company, says its new global network service, which will connect major cities in Japan, Asia, the U.S. and Europe, guarantees end-to-end quality services.

But while NTT hopes to secure the communications demands of high-margin corporate customers overseas, global telecoms giants in Europe and America have also been hoping to secure access to Japan's vast telecoms market.
Amid speculation that NTT might be discussing a closer relationship with Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc, Tomita noted only that NTT was talking to many carriers.

But he also denied NTT was much closer to BT and its Concert Communications alliance with America's MCI Communications Corp -- despite a 10-year relationship -- than other telecoms groups keen on boosting a presence in the booming Asian markets.

"I don't think we are very much closer to BT because the business we have made so far together is very small," Tomita said. "We are studying options on an equal basis. We are (also) in talks with C&W and some other European-based or U.S.-based carriers."

He said although NTT and C&W had a long relationship, partly through C&W's 17.5 percent stake in Japan's second biggest international carrier, International Digital Communications, NTT was not committed to what he called an "alliance-type relationship" with any of its suitors.
BT had hoped that its planned $20 billion merger with MCI would make it more a more attractive partner to the likes of NTT.

But just over two weeks ago, MCI issued a surprise profit warning that sent shares plunging and prompted BT to launch a full-scale review of the merger terms and the U.S. long distance carrier's operations and plans.

MCI blamed its expected losses on delays entering the $100 billion local U.S. telephone markets. It forecast losses of $800 million this year -- double previous estimates -- and possibly Although Tomita declined to comment on the BT/MCI merger, he said NTT sympathised with MCI's strategy of stepping up costly investments to break into local markets.
"We understand that MCI's (investment) strategy is very important," he said, adding it was important to control local networks amid diving international and long-distance call prices.
